 2   Q. Please state your name, position, and business address.

 3   A. My name is Alex Eubanks. I am the New Mexico Representative for the Southwest Energy

 4   Efficiency Project, or SWEEP. My business address is 2334 Broadway, Suite A, Boulder, Colorado

 5   80304. I am based in Albuquerque, New Mexico.

 6   Q. On whose behalf are you testifying in this proceeding?

 7   A. I am testifying on behalf of the Coalition for Clean Affordable Energy, or CCAE.

 8   Q. Please briefly describe the Southwest Energy Efficiency Project (“SWEEP”) and your role

 9   with the organization.

10   A. SWEEP is a nonprofit organization dedicated to advancing energy efficiency and related

11   clean energy policies across the Southwest. In New Mexico, my work focuses on utility policy

12   and regulatory matters, legislative advocacy, energy affordability, energy efficiency program

13   development, building decarbonization, and the implementation of federal and state energy

14   programs.

15   As SWEEP’s New Mexico Representative, I engage with a wide range of stakeholders, including

16   legislators, public utilities, state agencies, local governments, labor organizations, contractors,

17   community-based organizations, and advocacy groups. My responsibilities include developing,

18   evaluating, and supporting policy proposals; coordinating stakeholder engagement; assisting in

19   the implementation of energy programs; and analyzing utility policies, rate structures, and

20   customer-facing programs that affect New Mexico customers. My work includes evaluating

21   energy affordability programs and assessing their impacts on low and moderate income

22   households, including program design considerations within utility regulatory frameworks. In



                                                       1
  1   performing this work, I also draw on SWEEP’s broader organizational experience with utility

 2   regulation, energy efficiency, rate design, building decarbonization, and low-income customer

 3   programs across the Southwest.

 4   Q. Please summarize your professional background.

 5   A. I have approximately 17 years of experience in New Mexico public service, policy, advocacy,

 6   and stakeholder engagement. I joined SWEEP in March 2024. Since then, my work has included

 7   utility policy, low-income energy affordability, energy efficiency, building decarbonization,

 8   clean transportation, energy codes, contractor training, and implementation of federal and state

 9   energy programs. This work has included reviewing utility program proposals, participating in

10   stakeholder processes, and evaluating program design and implementation considerations

11   relevant to utility customers.

12   Before joining SWEEP, I worked for many years in the New Mexico office of U.S. Senator Martin

13   Heinrich. In that role, I engaged in environmental policy, public lands policy, home energy

14   efficiency policy and programs, federal program implementation, and stakeholder engagement. I

15   also helped New Mexicans navigate major federal programs, including pandemic-related

16   programs such as the Paycheck Protection Program, Economic Injury Disaster Loan program and

17   the Restaurant Revitalization Fund. That work required understanding program eligibility rules,

18   funding structures, agency processes, and practical implementation challenges.

19   Earlier in my career, from 2015-2017, I worked in New Mexico campaigns and public affairs,

20   including as a partner at Rio Strategies. That work included coalition-building, public

21   communication, candidate recruitment, campaign management, policy research, data analysis, and

22   stakeholder engagement.

23   Q. Please describe your educational background.

 2   Q. Are you currently undertaking any utility regulatory or ratemaking training relevant to

 3   your work?

 4   A. Yes. I am currently enrolled in the Spring 2026 National Association of Regulatory Utility

 5   Commissioners Rate School, which focuses on utility regulation, ratemaking principles, and

 6   program evaluation. I have begun the preliminary coursework, and the in-person portion of the

 7   training is scheduled for May 10 through May 15, 2026.

 8   Q. Do you have experience related to low-income utility rates in New Mexico?

 9   A. Yes. At SWEEP, I supported the organization’s work, in collaboration with coalition partners

10   and the bill sponsor, in advancing House Bill 91, which amended Section 62-8-6 NMSA 1978 to

11   authorize the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (“Commission”) to approve rates and

12   programs designed to reduce the energy burden for low-income customers.

13   That work is relevant to this proceeding because it gave me direct experience with the policy

14   framework governing low-income rate design in New Mexico, including program eligibility,

15   funding mechanisms, and the policy considerations underlying New Mexico Public Regulation

16   Commission approval of affordability programs. This experience is directly relevant to this

17   proceeding because Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS”) seeks approval of Rate No.

18   89, described as an Electric Affordability Program (“EAP”) for income-qualified residential

19   customers. My role in supporting HB 91 gave me direct experience with the policy purpose

20   behind low-income utility rate authority in New Mexico and with the importance of designing

21   programs that meaningfully reduce energy burdens for eligible customers. My work on HB 91

22   provided direct experience with the policy objectives of reducing customer energy burden and

23   the importance of designing programs that meaningfully achieve those outcomes for eligible

 3   another regulatory body?

 4   A. No. This is my first time submitting testimony before the Commission.

 5   Q. What is the basis for your testimony?

 6   A. My testimony is based on my professional experience, my review of relevant materials and

 7   utility filings in this proceeding, and my knowledge of energy affordability program design and

 8   implementation in New Mexico. While I am not offering engineering or cost-of-service

 9   modeling testimony, my expertise relates to program design, policy implementation, and

10   customer impacts of the EAP.

13                II.     PURPOSE AND SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS

14   Q. What is the purpose of your testimony?

15   A. The purpose of my testimony is to evaluate Southwestern Public Service Company’s

16   proposed Electric Affordability Program Rider, Rate No. 89, which I refer to as the EAP, and to



                                                     4
  1   provide recommendations to the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission regarding program

 2   design and implementation.

 3   My testimony evaluates the proposed program design, including eligibility, program reach,

 4   budget support, cost recovery, shareholder funding, reporting, and future program development.

 5   My testimony focuses on whether the proposed EAP is designed to meaningfully reduce energy

 6   burden for income-qualified customers and whether modifications are needed to improve

 7   program effectiveness, reach, and alignment with statutory objectives.

 8   I recommend that the Commission approve Rate No. 89 with modifications and conditions

 9   designed to improve program effectiveness, transparency, reach, and cost recovery. In my

10   professional opinion, the proposal is appropriate in concept and legally authorized, but SPS has

11   not provided enough current-case support for the program's proposed budget, expected reach,

12   and cost-recovery structure.

13   I do not offer engineering, cost-of-service, or testimony other than on the low-income rate. My

14   analysis focuses on EAP design, policy implementation, and customer impacts based on my

15   professional experience and review of the record in this proceeding.

16   Q. Why is SPS proposing the EAP in this case?

17   A. SPS is proposing the EAP under NMSA 1978, Section 62-8-6, as amended in 2025. That

18   statute now allows the Public Regulation Commission to approve rates and programs designed to

19   reduce the burden of energy costs on low-income customers. 1 SPS's Application specifically asks

20   the Commission to approve the EAP to assist income-eligible residential customers under

21   Section 62-8-6. 2

20   A. Based on the current record, I recommend that the Commission approve the proposed EAP in

21   concept, but require SPS to modify Rate No. 89 in five primary ways:

 7   efficiency, weatherization, and customer outreach programs. The EAP should not create new

10   Transportation Electrification Plan offerings, that can reduce bills over time.

11   Q. Do you recommend that the Commission reject the EAP?

12   A. No. I do not recommend that the Commission reject the EAP. I recommend that the

13   Commission approve Rate No. 89 with the modifications described in my testimony. Low-

14   income affordability assistance is needed, and the Commission now has express statutory

15   authority to approve rates and programs designed to reduce low-income energy burdens.

16   SPS did not perform a new budget analysis for the $750,000 program budget in this case, and

17   SPS states that it did not consider alternatives to the proposed cost-recovery method or allocation

18   methodology. 7 It is difficult to assess the real energy burden reduction under these

19   circumstances. Given the proposed rate increase and the limited expected reach of the program,

20   I recommend modifications and reporting requirements designed to make the program more

21   effective and better supported by current-case data.

 2   Q. Please summarize SPS's proposed Electric Affordability Program.

 3   A. SPS proposes to establish Rate No. 89, the Electric Affordability Program Rider, or EAP. The

 4   proposed EAP would be available to residential customers in SPS's New Mexico service territory

 5   who are qualified for and receive LIHEAP assistance during the applicable federal fiscal year.

 6   To be considered a Qualified Customer under the rider, the customer must also agree to be

 7   placed on SPS's Average Monthly Payment Plan, or AMPP, and must agree to a payment

 8   schedule. That payment schedule would require the customer to pay the current monthly bill

 9   after the application of the Affordability bill credit and, if applicable, to pay a portion of the

10   customer’s pre-EAP arrears. 8

11   The proposed program has two components: an Affordability Component and an Arrearage

12   Forgiveness Component. 9

15   rider states that the credit would be calculated as one-twelfth of the difference between SPS's

17   Department of Health and Human Services Poverty Guidelines for a household of four. 10

18   SPS proposes to provide supplemental assistance to Residential Service customers during June,

19   July, August, and September. For Residential Space Heating customers, SPS proposes to provide

20   supplemental assistance during November, December, January, and February. 11
